name: Benin

facts.religion: Christian about 52%, Muslim about 28%, Vodun and other traditional faiths

snapshot: The country that pioneered peaceful handovers in Africa held another in 2026, but with the main opposition kept off the ballot and jihadist attacks spreading in the north.
culture: Benin is the birthplace of Vodun, which has official recognition and a national holiday every 10 January in Ouidah, the old slave port where the Door of No Return now stands as a memorial. The kingdom of Dahomey, with its Agojie women soldiers, ruled the south for two centuries. Cotonou's art scene draws on that heritage, and the return of royal treasures looted by France in 1892 became a national event in 2021.
society: Cotton is the main export, and much of the economy runs on trade with Nigeria, formal and informal, through the port of Cotonou. Growth has been strong, but poverty remains widespread outside the south. Since 2021, jihadist groups from the Sahel have attacked army posts in the north near the Burkina Faso and Niger borders, killing dozens of soldiers in single raids.
situation: In 1991, Benin became the first country in mainland Africa where a sitting ruler lost an election and handed over power peacefully. For a generation it was held up as proof that the continent's "Big Man" era could end. In 2026 it held another orderly transfer of power, and almost nobody outside the government treated it as a celebration.

President Patrice Talon stepped down after two terms, as the constitution requires. His handpicked successor, finance minister Romuald Wadagni, won the 12 April election with 94.05 percent. His only opponent took under 6 percent because the main opposition party, Les Démocrates, was kept off the ballot (KAS). In January's parliamentary vote the same party fell short of a 20 percent threshold, leaving Talon's coalition with every seat (Al Jazeera). The vote came four months after a coup attempt in December 2025 that was put down with help from Nigerian troops, and with jihadists of JNIM pressing into the north, where they killed 54 soldiers at one post in 2025. Talon's defenders point to roads, ports and fiscal discipline; his critics point to rules rewritten since 2016 so that his camp could not lose. Benin shows that democracy can erode without a coup: through thresholds, candidate rules and an election whose result everyone knew in advance.
power: A presidential republic. The president is directly elected for five years with a two-term limit and heads the government; the National Assembly is elected by proportional representation with high party thresholds.
holders: President Romuald Wadagni, Talon's successor, in office since May 2026.
